prize_parts.citation: for incorporating firm heterogeneity and selection into trade theory, showing how productivity differences across firms shape who exports and invests abroad, how openness reallocates resources, and the gains from trade.

statement.case_for: My configuration does not change: a single-part B020 award to Helpman and Melitz. The exchange sharpened my reasoning but did not move it. The chair asks for a common weighting, so I state mine. I weigh (1) how much the contribution changed what economists can ask and measure, (2) durability under replication and extension, and (3) whether credit can be assigned defensibly. B020 does best on the first two. Selection into exporting moved the unit of analysis from the industry to the firm. It made within-industry reallocation a first-order channel for productivity gains from openness. It also gave firm-level and transaction-level data a theory to be estimated against, and it spread into industrial organisation and quantitative macro. Melitz (2003) is the conceptual core. Helpman, Melitz and Yeaple (2004) is the natural extension to exporting versus foreign direct investment. After more than two decades there is no maturity concern. It complements the 2008 recognition of new trade theory and does not repeat it. On the third criterion B020 is weaker than B001, and I weigh that openly. My answer to the chair's first question is that the omission of Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum from the credited list is a real risk but not disqualifying. The model of selection is most clearly Melitz's, and Helpman's extension is the natural second name. The citation should say what is credited, the theoretical framework of firm heterogeneity and selection, and should not imply that the empirical firm-level literature is exhausted. The Scientific Background can set out the empirical precursors fully. My answer to the third question is that I would accept either B020 or B001 as a single-part trade award, with B020 clearly first for me. I would not combine them, because crediting Helpman in two parts would credit one person twice for overlapping fields.
statement.case_against: The attribution gap is the main weakness, and the discussion did not close it. Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum are close to the core and cannot be added to a configuration built from the credited list. A Helpman-Melitz award could be read as under-crediting the empirical origins of the field, and B001 does not carry that risk. The gains-from-trade results also depend on parametric assumptions such as Pareto productivity and CES demand, so the quantitative welfare claims are less secure than the qualitative mechanism. Helpman's overlap with B001 forces the Committee to choose which of his bodies of work it recognises. If colleagues give priority to a clean two-person attribution or to doubts about the parametric welfare results, B001 is a defensible alternative. Redding's quantitative and spatial extensions are real and I leave them out. That is a judgement about the originating step, not a claim that they are unimportant.

responses.point: Hassler asks that the case for B020 be stated directly against B001 before deciding whether it moves above his third-ranked candidate. He also stresses that the 2008 timing argument is about balance and not merit, and that Helpman's overlap should not make either route easier.
responses.response: I agree that the 2008 gap says nothing about merit and that Helpman should not serve as a bridge for either candidate, so I do not rely on either. Head to head, both are mature. B001 has the cleaner attribution and a durable framework. B020 has the larger effect on empirical practice: the selection and reallocation mechanisms were confronted with firm-level data in many countries and changed how trade is estimated and how policy is evaluated. Mixed test results for protection for sale do not show it failed, but they do mean its influence runs ahead of its confirmation. The cost is that B020 has the weaker attribution. That is why I call B001 a close alternative and not a distant one. You and I are co-authors, so you should not count my agreement or disagreement with you as independent evidence.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson ranks B001 first. She argues that mixed results for protection for sale are the normal fate of a testable framework and mean 'contested magnitudes', not 'no lasting contribution'. She also notes that B020 has an attribution gap (Redding, Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum) that B001 lacks.
responses.response: I accept the distinction between contested magnitudes and no lasting contribution, and I do not say B001 lacks one. We differ on weighting, and my view is that B020 changed more of what empirical economists do. On attribution you are right that B001 is cleaner, and I count that on your side. But a cleaner attribution does not mean a larger contribution. The gap in B020 is one I can address in the citation wording and the Scientific Background, whereas I cannot repair it by adding uncredited names. If the Committee judges the gap more serious than I do, I would move to B001 before any other candidate, and that is why it is my first alternative.

responses.point: Teorell ranks B001 first and B020 as his first alternative. He ranks B020 lower because omitting the empirical firm-level pioneers would invite a priority dispute that the Grossman-Helpman pairing avoids. He wants a clear argument for why Melitz and Helpman, and not a wider group, define the contribution.
responses.response: I take that challenge seriously and will answer it directly. The reason the pair defines the contribution is that the conceptual step, the model of selection into exporting, is Melitz's. Helpman, Melitz and Yeaple extended it to the exporting-versus-FDI margin. The empirical firm-level facts and related models from Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum are precursors and parallel work that the Scientific Background should describe. I hold this with moderate confidence, because the boundary is a judgement and not an uncontested fact. I agree with you that B001 should stand on its own case and not on Helpman's credit elsewhere. For that reason I treat the choice between B001 and B020 as a single decision about which strand to honour.

responses.point: Krusell ranks B016 first with moderate confidence and calls B001 the closest rival. He now accepts the two-name Kiyotaki-Moore version of B031, because adding Gertler would blur attribution given the prior laureate on the financial accelerator.
responses.response: I agree on B031: Kiyotaki and Moore is the cleaner attribution, and I keep it as a second alternative only, because the 2022 prize reduces its marginal case. On B016, I remain where I was in round 1. I rank it third because of the 2024 overlap and the identification problem in constitutional comparisons, and your point that the later literature moved to better within-country designs does not fully resolve that for me. I do not count your first place for B016 as an argument against B020. We are frequent co-authors, so my disagreement with you is not independent evidence either way.

uncertainties: Whether the Committee treats the omission of Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum as disqualifying. I do not, but I hold that view with moderate confidence and it may be the deciding factor.
Whether the Committee recognises Helpman through the firm-heterogeneity strand (B020) or the political-economy and growth strand (B001), and whether it would accept either as a single-part award.
How robust the gains-from-trade results are to alternative productivity distributions and demand assumptions, and how much that should count against the empirical side of the case.
Whether Redding's quantitative and spatial extensions belong in a third seat. I think not, but a colleague could reasonably disagree.
My assessment of priority and attribution relies on recollection and the written exchange. I have not independently verified citations or priority claims.
statement.conflict_note: The profile shows no connection to Helpman or Melitz, the credited names in my preferred part. It also shows none to Grossman (B001) or to Kiyotaki and Moore (B031), my alternatives. Other connections remain as disclosed in round 1 and are not adjudicated. I have a long-running collaboration with Peter Klenow, who is credited on B036, which is not part of my configuration. I have collaborated with Aghion, Bergeaud and Li, none of whom is credited on any shortlisted entry that I rely on. I am a frequent co-author of committee colleague Krusell (secretary) and a co-author of the chair, Hassler. Both prefer B016, which I ranked third, so my replies to them should not be read as independent evidence. My IIES affiliation and Stockholm ties are with committee colleagues and not with any credited candidate.
